sources.title: Gemini 4 Argon: Built to solve your hardest problems
sources.text: We’re giving developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers access to our latest frontier model. SVP, Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect, Google Your browser does not support the audio element. Gemini 4 Argon is now globally available today for developers and enterprises via the API in AI Studio and Gemini platform , for Google AI Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity , and Google AI Ultra and Pro subscribers in the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search . Argon excels at deep work in complex, real-world tasks across domains including coding, finance, legal, cybersecurity, and science. Its depth and precision across multi-step tasks leads Argon to outperform other frontier models on benchmarks across domains , ranking #1 on the Vals Index , which measures model performance across critical economic sectors like finance, coding, legal, and tax work. The model launches today at an introductory price 1 of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens (with cached input tokens at 95% off). Teams at Google, across enterprises, and in the research community have already been using Argon to land significant impact across fields: At Google, we’ve been using Argon on our hardest engineering problems. Over the past few weeks, software engineers have been shipping high-quality code faster than ever. Argon in Antigravity has helped teams increase agentic code submissions by more than 35% while reducing code rollbacks by nearly a third. Argon built a highly detailed model of a Pagoda using multi-agent visual critique loops in Antigravity. The model autonomously sculpted a multi-building temple complex with photorealistic architecture, foliage and lighting in Blender. Argon turned pictures of a real desk into a playable miniature racing game using a multi-agent loop in Antigravity. The desk objects, room and race track were modeled and collision-checked using Blender MCP, textured with Nano Banana, and wired with physics, custom shaders, and car engine audio from Gemini Omni Flash in Three.js. Try it now in Google AI Studio. Argon in Antigravity wrote Python scripts to procedurally sculpt, rig, animate, and PBR-bake a complex 3D game using multi-agent visual critique loops then wired it for the web in Three.js with GLSL shaders, shatter physics, and a single-player AI. Try it now in Google AI Studio. With zero external libraries and 100% pure Python, Argon wrote its own 3D ray-tracing engine with a custom video tool and audio mixer to build and document a sunlit library from scratch, producing, narrating, and assembling this video with Gemini 3.8 TTS voiceover and music by Lyria 3.5. View the source code . Starting from a single Nano Banana image in Antigravity, Argon drives Blender MCP in an autonomous loop, aligning camera grids, sculpting Gothic architecture, and staging audio-reactive lighting, to create a finished 3D scene. Argon combines frontier reasoning, deep visual perception, expanded domain knowledge, and stronger writing capabilities across legal, finance, science, and coding to help with high-stakes professional workflows. It communicates clearly, keeping you in the loop, and follows style instructions better than any of our previous Gemini models. Argon answers questions more directly with less hedging, doesn’t repeat itself more than necessary, and skips clichés throughout the responses. Enterprise customers and startups in our early access program are already seeing strong wins with Argon. Using its advanced reasoning and multimodal capabilities while maintaining strict grounding, Argon excels in deep multimodal document comprehension, longitudinal data analysis, and interactive analytical sandboxes. See how Argon synthesizes ~50 GB of Airborne LiDAR scans, GIS room vectors, Library of Congress CAD drawings, and NPS archives to reconstruct 3D models of Chaco Canyon, turning fragmented archaeological records into explorable digital heritage sites. Try it now in Google AI Studio. In Gemini App, Argon takes an unstructured folder full of project context and formats it into a clean proposal deck for a client using a custom skill. Gemini then drafts and emails the deck to a client while creating an automated workflow for all future incoming client requests with a scheduled task. Watch Argon synthesize data from 3 open-source repositories into a medical learning tool where you can peel back anatomical layers, inspect clinical metadata, and trigger biomechanics in a 3D exploration of the human body. Argon using Antigravity in the Gemini macOS app generates design iterations for new legs for a sofa using Nano Banana then generates a 3d printable file for one. Starting from a sketch of the measurements and a photo of the couch Argon builds the model to the correct size to fit the sofa. At Isomorphic Labs, the team is using Argon as a partner to accelerate their drug discovery and design research workflows. Argon is able to quickly synthesize complex PDFs and patents to extract pertinent information, reducing a process that typically takes weeks into hours. Researchers, engineers, and security specialists are already using Argon to push the boundaries of cyber defense, science, math, and robotics. It’s helping cyber defenders and researchers test hypotheses, autonomously audit critical codebases and formal proofs, and catch subtle zero-day vulnerabilities and logic flaws. Starting today, we’re beginning expansion to hundreds of additional Fairwind Program partners. Wiz is already using Argon for its " Scan for Good " initiative, which protects critical infrastructure for the public good and for free. With early access to the model, Wiz has demonstrated Argon's real-world impact across multiple high-stakes sectors: Argon is already having real-world impact across the scientific community — enabling novel discovery for scientists and experts across multiple domains. To further advance the pace of research, we’re offering 10,000 scientists the highest usage tier in Google Antigr

sources.title: Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics
sources.text: Gemini 4 Argon marks a step change in physical understanding, code generation, and visual-semantic reasoning—unlocking new workflows across the robotics stack and accelerating progress toward physical AGI. You can see this leap in capability on the Embodied Reasoning (ERQA) benchmark , which tests a model's ability to understand and solve physical, spatial problems in 3D environments. Using pure reasoning, Argon scores 87%, outperforming every other frontier model. As a general-purpose physical reasoning model, Argon can be applied across the entire robotics lifecycle. In this post, we share representative prompts for Argon across four key areas: Argon controls a Boston Dynamics Spot® quadruped (12-DoF legs + 6-DoF arm) to learn a new skill: stepping on a foot-pedal trash bin to throw away soda cans. Argon creates an articulated MuJoCo digital twin of a foot-pedal trash bin to practice its moves before stepping on the physical pedal and dropping soda cans into the open bin. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Argon controls a simple robotic arm to place a fallen mug upright and put the crumpled napkin inside. Argon reasons with a visual coordinate harness and action primitives to perform this task over several turns. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Argon steers robots in the Gemini Omni World Model to rearrange five scattered Scrabble tiles ( G, R, A, N, O ) into a clean row spelling A - R - G - O - N . Instead of specifying one static prompt, Argon steers in a closed visual loop. It writes timestamped action prompts, inspecting intermediate rollout keyframes, and refining its prompts. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Argon views a real robot teleoperation episode and develops a digital twin; it obtains or creates simulation assets that look and behave like the real objects upon contact with the dexterous hands. Argon tunes the assets and scenes to match sim visuals and contact events with those in the real recorded data in an iterative visual-reasoning loop. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Given an egocentric human video of a manipulation task, Argon identifies the task-relevant objects, replaces crude bounding boxes with compound convex-decomposed meshes for concave containers, and retargets the human hand trajectory onto a 76-DoF bimanual humanoid with 22-DoF five-fingered hands in MuJoCo contact physics. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video With Argon, a developer can snap a photo of a rough pen-and-paper sketch—showing an Apollo 2 humanoid throwing a ball along a parabolic arc to topple a 3-2-1 stack of boxes on a table—and have Argon automatically construct the GPU-accelerated mujoco_warp scene, synthesize a balanced 76-DoF whole-body and five-finger throw trajectory, verify 6/6 target knockdown in closed-loop physics, and export a Blender 4.5 Cycles render. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Argon has precise physical understanding of dexterous manipulation and can provide detailed segmentation and text labeling from video. Argon is able to identify poor manipulation segments such as pauses, unstable grasps and fumbles. Given an overhead video of a bimanual ALOHA 2 robot folding a square sheet of paper into an origami fox over 136 seconds, Argon produces a time-aligned 4-level hindsight annotation hierarchy: Episode Goal (G1), 6 contiguous Semantic Subtasks (G2), 17 contact-level Atomic Primitives (G3), and automated Quality Control (QC) reweighting that holds task progress flat during fumbles and retries. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video To recreate the classic 12-ball balance scale puzzle with robots, Argon builds a bimanual Franka FR3 MuJoCo environment with 12 visually identical pool balls (one secretly heavier or lighter) and an articulated Roberval two-pan balance scale. It then writes a vision-only closed-loop solver that triangulates the balls from stereo RGB cameras, visually reads the scale tilt after each weighing, and isolates the odd ball into the Heavy (Red) or Light (Blue) tray within 3 weighings. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Argon is a general value function for robotics tasks. Evaluated on a 60-second bimanual ring-sorting episode from a human UMI dataset, Argon iteratively inspects synchronized head, left-gripper, and right-gripper camera feeds around contact transitions to generate dense value function / task progress predictions and decompose the trajectory into 28 segments with positive, neutral, and negative progress slopes. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Argon can generate new data in simulation to improve performance of generalist vision-language-action (VLA) models. Starting from a single RGB photo of the real tabletop, Argon autonomously builds a calibrated MuJoCo simulation twin, defines new tasks, and synthesizes a closed-loop motion generator to collect 4,500+ domain-randomized episodes in simulation—boosting real-world physical robot Success Rate from 56% to 75% and reducing completion time from 35s to 24s . Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video On a simple 6-DoF arm, Argon iteratively self-improves both execution speed and placement accuracy on a pick and place task via trial and self-reflection. sources.name: Roboflow
sources.title: Use Gemini 4 Argon to build computer vision applications
sources.text: Today we added Gemini 4 Argon, Google’s newest multimodal model, to Roboflow. As of this writing, it ranks first on Roboflow Playground , where we compare vision models on real-world tasks, for object detection, counting, and text extraction. Roboflow is a platform for building computer vision applications, from labeling images and training models to deploying them in the cloud or on your hardware. With Gemini 4 Argon in Roboflow, you can label hundreds of images automatically to train a model that’s fast enough for live video, or use Argon as one step in an application that combines several models. Gemini 4 Argon is the newest multimodal model from Google. You give it an image and instructions in plain language, and it returns text, structured data, or bounding boxes around the objects you ask for. In our evaluations, it’s especially good at three tasks that come up often in vision applications: finding objects, counting them, and reading text in real-world images from manufacturing, logistics, and aerial imagery. Every advance in frontier models expands what’s possible with computer vision. Gemini 4 Argon is another step toward applications that understand more of the world, solve more ambitious problems, and improve as the underlying models improve. Our vision for Roboflow is to be the vision harness that turns those advances into better applications: a foundation for evaluating new capabilities, combining frontier and specialized models, and routing each task to the right model. The goal is to keep customers at the frontier of what’s possible across accuracy, speed, and cost, with the freedom to adopt better models from any provider, without vendor lock-in. Auto Label and Workflows are two starting points, which you can use to build vision systems that keep getting better: stronger evaluations, more capable reasoning, and better ways to put each new breakthrough to work. Auto Label draws labels on a whole batch of images for you. You list the objects you want labeled, with a short description of each, and Gemini 4 Argon finds every match and draws a bounding box around it. That way, you can label hundreds of images without drawing each box by hand and spend your time reviewing the results instead. Those labels become training data for a specialized model. Gemini 4 Argon can find objects from a written description, but a model of its size is too slow and costly to run on every frame of a live video. A model like RF-DETR , trained on your images, runs in real time on edge devices like NVIDIA Jetson. With Auto Label, Argon labels the training data, and RF-DETR runs on your cameras in production. For example, let’s say you operate a quarry and want to know how your equipment is used across a shift, like how many loads each wheel loader moves and how long dump trucks wait to be filled. You pull a few hundred frames from drone footage of the site, list classes like haul truck, dump truck, wheel loader, excavator, and screening plant, and run Auto Label with Gemini 4 Argon. After you review the labels, you train an RF-DETR model that tracks every vehicle on the site, frame by frame. Gemini 4 Argon is available in Auto Label on object detection projects, in Label Assist in the annotation editor, and through Roboflow Agent . You can also start Auto Label jobs with it from the Roboflow API, the Roboflow MCP server , and the Python SDK by setting the model type to gemini-4-argon-boxes. On paid plans, it’s now the default model for object detection labeling, so Auto Label selects it for you. Workflows are how you build vision applications in Roboflow. You connect models and logic as steps, then run the result in the cloud or on your hardware. Some use cases might need more than a detector can provide, like reading a serial number or answering a question about what’s happening in a scene. Gemini 4 Argon is now a model option in the Google Gemini block , so you can add those steps to your Workflows. A large multimodal model takes longer and costs more per image than a specialized detector, so it pays to use it selectively. A common pattern is to run an efficient detector like RF-DETR on every frame of a video, then send Argon only the frames where a product is in position under the camera, or crops of the specific components you need to verify. That way, the detector covers every frame at full speed, and Argon reads and reasons only where your application needs it. For example, let’s say you inspect motherboards after assembly and need to confirm that every capacitor matches the bill of materials (BOM). A detection model finds each capacitor on the board, and a Dynamic Crop step cuts each one out of the image. Gemini 4 Argon reads the capacitance and voltage rating printed on each capacitor and returns them as JSON fields. A final step compares the values against the BOM, flags the board for rework when a capacitor has the wrong rating, and sends it to a technician when a marking isn’t readable. The Google Gemini block supports these task types with Gemini 4 Argon: Detection and classification results use the same format as other Roboflow models, so they connect directly to blocks like visualizations, counting, and filters. You can also set a thinking level for each step, using a low level for quick answers and a high level when a task needs more reasoning. Workflows with Gemini 4 Argon run in the Roboflow cloud starting today, through the Serverless API . Support for self-hosted inference servers will follow in an upcoming release of Roboflow Inference. By default, the block uses Roboflow’s managed key and bills Gemini token use to your Roboflow credits. You can also provide a Google AI API key and pay Google directly. Gemini 4 Argon lets you describe what you need in plain language and get back boxes, counts, and text. In Roboflow, you can put that to work in two ways: labeling the training data for a fast, specialized model, or handling the steps in a Workflow that need to read and reason about

sources.title: Google finally releases Gemini 4 Argon
sources.text: After months of trailing its rivals, Google says Argon competes with the industry’s best. After months of trailing its rivals, Google says Argon competes with the industry’s best. After months sitting on the sidelines of the frontier AI race, Google has finally launched its long-awaited Gemini 4 Argon model, claiming it can compete with the best the industry has to offer. Google says Argon delivers “frontier reasoning and improved performance across complex workflows,” while cutting down on hedging, repetition, and the cliches that continue to plague AI chatbots. The company claims Argon outperforms rival models like GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable 5.1, and Claude Opus 5.5 across a range of benchmarks, including coding, cybersecurity, science, finance, and law. Google says it’s already putting Argon to use internally, such as finding and patching cybersecurity vulnerabilities, halving the computing power needed to power YouTube’s comments section, and debugging the drone physics simulator for Alphabet’s drone delivery company Wing. The model is rolling out today to Google’s higher-tier Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app and AI mode in Search, as well to Ultra subscribers on its agentic development platform Antigravity. It is not clear when — or if — Argon will be available to Plus subscribers or free users. Google is pricing Argon very competitively. The model is launching with an introductory price of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, around a fifth the cost of OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra and Anthropic’s Fable 5 models. Even after those costs double at the end November — when the introductory period finishes — Argon will still be significantly cheaper than its frontier rivals on a per-token basis, though this doesn’t necessarily translate to lower costs in practice, as models can use different numbers of tokens for the same tasks. The launch fills in some of the blanks left behind from when Google first teased Argon a few weeks ago. In line with other recent frontier model releases, the public rollout follows a limited release to a select set of “trusted cyber defenders” to be tested for potential risks. Argon is Google’s first major frontier release since Gemini 3 in late 2025. In the intervening months, impressive models from Anthropic and OpenAI have seen Google trail far behind its rivals. Seismic internal shakeups raised further doubts about the company’s ability — or desire — to reclaim its position and compete at the frontier of AI. But Argon’s arrival suggests we can’t count Google out of the AI race just yet. Landing just a day after Meta announced its own frontier model , Muse Wonder Full, Argon is a reminder of how quickly the balance of power can shift in AI, and that the frontier is far from a two-horse race.

sources.title: Google's Gemini 4 Argon is now available in the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search
sources.text: But only Google AI Ultra and Pro subscribers can access it for now. Google's latest AI model, Gemini 4 Argon , is now available for more people. It first rolled out to members of Google's Fairwind Program, made up of governments and trusted partners that need access to the company's models with the most advanced cybersecurity capabilities, earlier this month. Now, developers can access it via the Gemini API and Google's agentic software developer platform Antigravity, while Google AI Ultra and Pro subscribers will be able to use it through the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search. In the US, Google AI Pro costs $20 a month, while the Ultra tier costs at least $100. Access to Argon will set users back $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. But those are just introductory prices valid until November 30. After that, Argon will cost users double those amounts. Google was supposed to launch a 3.5 Pro model, but it moved on and released Argon instead. The company said during its launch that the model can handle complex tasks involving finance, software engineering, coding, creative writing and cybersecurity defense. According to AI benchmarking company Artificial Analysis, Gemini 4 Argon matches OpenAI GPT-6 Astra's score for its Intelligence Index, which is its composite score for multiple AI benchmarks, at 60 percent of the cost per task at its introductory prices. Josh Woodward, VP of Product for Gemini and Google Labs, said that in the Gemini app, Argon answers more quickly and with less hedging, repetitions and clichés. It can also return responses while it's still thinking when dealing with longer tasks that would usually mean waiting a bit — or a long while, depending on the AI being used — for results. Google is also making it easier to toggle between chat and tasks within the Gemini app. Plus, it's adding Antigravity's agentic coding interface inside Gemini's macOS app.

sources.title: Gemini 4 Argon es la nueva bestia de Google para el trabajo pesado: código, ciencia, finanzas y ciberseguridad
sources.text: Imaginemos que encargamos a una inteligencia artificial una tarea que no puede resolverse con una sola respuesta: revisar miles de líneas de código, detectar qué partes ralentizan un programa y proponer cambios sin alterar su funcionamiento. El reto no consiste únicamente en comprender la petición, sino en sostener un trabajo de varias etapas y comprobar que cada decisión encaja con las anteriores. Esa misma dificultad aparece, con otras exigencias, cuando hay que interpretar informes financieros o examinar sistemas informáticos en busca de vulnerabilidades. Son problemas en los que responder rápido importa bastante menos que llegar a resultados fiables. Detrás de esta apuesta está Gemini 4 Argon , el nuevo modelo de Google DeepMind con el que la compañía busca reforzar sus capacidades para el trabajo especializado. No se trata exactamente de un estreno: fue anunciado el 30 de septiembre, cuando su utilización quedó reservada a determinados expertos en ciberseguridad mediante el programa Fairwind. La novedad es que Google ha comenzado su despliegue global para desarrolladores, empresas y suscriptores de determinados planes de pago. Con este movimiento, el gigante tecnológico pone el foco en cuatro grandes campos de aplicación: programación, finanzas, investigación científica y seguridad informática. Para abordar estos trabajos, Google ha combinado en Argon capacidades de razonamiento avanzado, análisis de información visual y utilización de herramientas. El modelo puede examinar documentos y desarrollar operaciones que requieren varios pasos, apoyándose en un límite unificado de hasta un millón de tokens , las unidades con las que procesa y genera contenido. Hay un matiz importante: esta capacidad se comparte entre la información recibida, el razonamiento y la salida. Además, cada petición individual tiene límites inferiores, por lo que la compañía ha incorporado un mecanismo de continuación que permite completar procesos más extensos. Hay un ejemplo que permite entender mejor hasta dónde llegan estas capacidades. En una prueba interna con Agent Development Kit (ADK), un proyecto de Python de unas 205.000 líneas, Argon trabajó durante once horas y planteó seis optimizaciones. Tras revisarlas, Google descartó cuatro por posibles problemas de funcionamiento o por ofrecer mejoras de utilidad limitada, pero incorporó las dos restantes. Estas redujeron cerca de un 40% el tiempo de preparación de sesiones largas en memoria y un 21% el de importación del paquete. La compañía también atribuye al modelo una reorganización de cientos de archivos de Chromium, el proyecto en el que se basa Chrome. En el ámbito financiero, las aplicaciones van desde elaborar estados financieros de varios ejercicios hasta valorar empresas a partir de documentos presentados ante los reguladores. Kepler asegura que , durante sus evaluaciones, Gemini 4 Argon coincidió con los modelos de referencia elaborados por sus analistas en más del 99% de las cifras examinadas. En ciberseguridad, Google afirma que Wiz, una compañía especializada en este sector, utilizó el sistema para ayudar a detectar y corregir una vulnerabilidad que podía comprometer información privada de pacientes. Conviene matizar que estos resultados proceden de empresas colaboradoras y que las investigaciones de Wiz también cuentan con otras herramientas y especialistas humanos. La investigación científica ofrece otros ejemplos interesantes de lo que Google está consiguiendo con esta tecnología. En el diseño de enzimas, el sistema ayudó a crear cinco nuevos diseños de proteínas capaces de facilitar determinadas reacciones químicas. Según la compañía, los ensayos posteriores de laboratorio confirmaron que todos presentaban actividad catalítica. También participó en la optimización de una versión interna de AlphaQubit, su sistema de corrección de errores para computación cuántica, consiguiendo casi duplicar el rendimiento de inferencia de uno de sus componentes. Fuera de las demostraciones de Google, también encontramos evaluaciones independientes que permiten situar a Argon frente a sus competidores. En el Vals Index , una clasificación que mide el rendimiento en tareas profesionales de programación, finanzas, derecho y fiscalidad, el modelo ocupa el primer puesto con un 68,90% . Sin embargo, Artificial Analysis otorga 53 puntos a su configuración High en el índice general de capacidades, donde aparece en octava posición. La disponibilidad global no significa que cualquiera pueda utilizarlo gratis. Google lo ofrece en la aplicación Gemini y en el modo IA del buscador a los suscriptores de Google AI Pro y Ultra, mientras que los desarrolladores pueden acceder mediante la API de pago. Para utilizar Argon en Antigravity, los usuarios particulares necesitan una suscripción Ultra. La tarifa introductoria de la API es de 2 dólares por millón de tokens de entrada y 10 por millón de salida, cantidades que se duplicarán a partir del 1 de diciembre. La cuestión ahora es cómo rendirá fuera de las pruebas controladas y ante necesidades profesionales concretas. sources.title: Microsoft to expand Maia chip for the AI era
sources.text: Oct 12, 2026 | Scott Guthrie - Executive Vice President, Cloud + AI As we move into the era of Super Intelligence, Microsoft is entering a new phase of infrastructure. We will scale our Azure Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027, making Maia the primary inference system for Microsoft products and services. The multigenerational Azure Maia program has become a foundational element of Microsoft’s AI infrastructure strategy. Maia 200 is now serving Microsoft production workloads, including Microsoft Copilot , and supporting the MAI team as they develop next-generation models, with GitHub Copilot and Microsoft Foundry to follow by end of year. Across these workloads, Maia 200 runs OpenAI models , Microsoft’s own MAI models and leading open-source model families. Insights from the scale of Microsoft’s AI services allow for unique co-design between hardware systems and software applications to optimize real-world use cases across enterprise applications and industry scenarios. Maia 300 is a complete intelligent system designed for the new types of AI workloads emerging today: Long-context reasoning, latency-sensitive conversational experiences and sustained, multi-step agentic tasks. By improving efficiency across the system, we expect Maia 300 to deliver 40% more tokens per megawatt compared to leading GPU-based systems. And in a full 96-accelerator configuration, it delivers up to 7x the rack-scale token throughput of Maia 200. The Azure Maia system is designed around the real-world workloads Microsoft runs at scale and the models we expect to build in the years ahead. Because silicon development takes years, our software and hardware teams collaborate early to anticipate architectures, scale and capabilities, translating those requirements into greater memory capacity, higher bandwidth and more accelerators operating as a single system. That co-engineering is already delivering measurable efficiency gains. Maia 200 is deploying across the United States, Europe and Australia and delivering up to 1.7x more tokens per watt for built-in AI capabilities in Microsoft Teams, Copilot and Cowork experiences compared with leading GPU infrastructure. Experience running our AI models and services on Maia 200 directly informed the design of Maia 300. Together, the two generations are designed to support a broad set of additional Microsoft’s AI services: multi-step agentic work that will help GitHub deliver coding experiences more efficiently; cloud-scale model serving that will help Microsoft Foundry support diverse architectures and deployment environments; inference and data generation for the MAI team; and latency-sensitive interactions that will help Dragon Copilot scale workflows and reduce clinicians’ administrative burden. AI is becoming a foundational layer of every application, workflow and business process. As enterprises move beyond chat experiences to systems of agents that can reason, act and collaborate, AI infrastructure must deliver intelligence securely and efficiently at scale while continuously adapting as models and workloads evolve. As the third generation of our Azure Maia program, Maia 300 is designed with an inference-first architecture optimized for long-context, memory-intensive and decode-heavy AI workloads. This involves balancing compute, memory bandwidth, networking and power efficiency at cloud scale. Key capabilities of the Maia 300 system include: Less data movement, more useful compute: Moving data efficiently, rather than raw compute power, is increasingly the bottleneck in large inference systems. Maia 300’s software-defined dataflow architecture and AI-assisted kernel optimization work together to maximize locality, reduce data movement and improve utilization across compute, memory and networking resources. By treating dataflow as a first-class design principle, Maia 300 delivers a significant performance-per-watt advantage over traditional GPU architectures. Higher memory bandwidth within every watt: As AI workloads become increasingly context and memory-bound, Maia 300 delivers industry-leading HBM bandwidth per watt. Eight HBM4 stacks provide 18.0 TB/s of peak memory bandwidth within a 950-watt TDP, enabling efficient execution of large models and long-context workloads. Specialized kernel support uses on-die SRAM as a software-managed scratchpad, reducing pressure on HBM. Chiplet architecture for enhanced efficiency: A new multi-chiplet architecture separates compute, memory-controller and I/O functions, improving efficiency, scalability and cost structure. Compute chiplets are built on TSMC’s N2P process node to maximize performance-per-watt. Larger context, richer intelligence: By designing for advanced low-precision formats, including enhanced MXFP4, Maia 300 reduces memory and bandwidth requirements for both computation and KV-cache storage. The result is larger context windows, higher throughput and improved model efficiency within the same power envelope. Scale-up networking at datacenter scale: Maia 300 treats networking as a seamless extension of the software-defined dataflow architecture. Rather than moving data through separate communication layers, dataflow operations span compute, memory and network resources as a single system. High-bandwidth interconnects between Maia accelerators are optimized for tensor parallelism, while a custom AI transport delivers performant and reliable scale-up communication across accelerators and racks. The AI-optimized transport leverages Ethernet-based networking infrastructure to enable a unified topology that scales efficiently from a single rack to datacenter-scale deployments. Higher AI throughput from every rack: Maia 300 rack systems bring together 96 accelerators within a 167-kilowatt power envelope, delivering 27.6 TB of HBM capacity and 1.7 PB/s of aggregate HBM bandwidth across a high-speed scale-up domain. sources.text: The new Maia 300 chip will start rolling out to production AI workloads in 2027. The new Maia 300 chip will start rolling out to production AI workloads in 2027. Microsoft is announcing its third-generation Maia in-house AI chip today, designed to be the “primary AI inference system” for Microsoft’s products and services. Maia 300 not only improves the cost and efficiency of running AI workloads in the cloud, it’s also more capable of handling the latest reasoning models and agentic tasks. Maia 300 will start being rolled out to production in 2027, and it has been designed with efficiency in mind. “We expect Maia 300 to deliver 40 percent more tokens per megawatt compared to leading GPU-based systems,” says Scott Guthrie , executive vice president of Microsoft’s cloud group. “And in a full 96-accelerator configuration, it delivers up to 7x the rack-scale token throughput of Maia 200.” These efficiency improvements will allow Microsoft to rely mainly on its in-house AI chips soon, instead of ones from Nvidia and AMD. “We will scale our Azure Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027, making Maia the primary AI inference system for Microsoft products and services,” says Guthrie. Maia 300 is a successor to the 200, which was only announced in January . Maia 200 is already running on production AI workloads across Microsoft, including Microsoft Copilot, GitHub Copilot, Microsoft Foundry, and Microsoft’s own AI models. “Maia 200 is the best performing AI infrastructure in our fleet, measured in real world metrics for AI services,” says Guthrie. “Maia 300 is a complete AI system designed for the new types of AI workloads emerging today: Long-context reasoning, latency-sensitive conversational experiences, and sustained, multi-step agentic tasks.” Microsoft is using a new chiplet architecture to get its all-important efficiency gains. Built on TSMC’s N2P process node, the latest Maia 300 architecture separates compute, memory controller, and I/O functions. “This increases the silicon area dedicated to compute performance and allows each function to use the technology best suited to its role,” says the Azure hardware and infrastructure team. Maia 300 is also a key part of Microsoft’s own AI model work, and could help the company achieve its goal of catching up with Google DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic. “We have to work across the full stack, all the way down to the silicon,” says Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman. “At that scale we need a platform that we own, and that we co-design with our models. That’s why running our Microsoft AI models on top of the Maia chip is a critical focus for our team.”

sources.title: Meta presenta Muse Wonder, la IA que quiere destronar a Claude y ChatGPT
sources.text: Meta ha presentado Muse Wonder y Muse Wonder Full , sus modelos de inteligencia artificial más avanzados hasta la fecha. Tras años de mantenerse en los últimos lugares de la carrera de la IA, el gigante tecnológico por fin cierra la brecha con dos modelos que pueden competirle de frente a Claude y ChatGPT en todo tipo de tareas de agentes. Meta afirma que esta IA es un paso importante en su estrategia de crear asistentes capaces de ayudar en tareas complejas del trabajo y la vida cotidiana. Según la compañía, Muse Wonder y Muse Wonder Full tienen un rendimiento puntero en tareas agénticas , es decir, aquellas en las que la IA actúa de forma autónoma. Meta ha presentado a sus modelos como sucesores de Muse Spark y se posicionan en algo que la empresa define como superinteligencia personal. Esto podría generar conflicto entre muchos usuarios, ya que la industria está tomando un giro en cuanto a las definiciones y muchas empresas comienzan a adoptar el término "superinteligencia" popularizado hace unos días por Donald Trump. Pero lo que importa con Muse Wonder son sus capacidades y aquí el modelo destaca en dos frentes. Primero, Meta implementó una característica llamada Active Memory, con la cual el modelo recuerda información importante del usuario y la recupera cuando resulta útil para la tarea que necesita resolver. La segunda es Active Focus, que mantiene el esfuerzo en tareas largas y prueba enfoques alternativos o le pregunta al usuario antes de ejecutar acciones relevantes. A diferencia de Muse Spark, Wonder y Wonder Full están diseñados para actuar como agentes que realizan tareas complejas, utilizando contexto personal y profesional. Ambos se desempeñan de manera notable en áreas como razonamiento, memoria, programación y desarrollo de software. Meta señala que su IA tiene capacidad de trabajar con información jurídica, financiera y de salud , ya que ha sido entrenada con conocimientos especializados y puede seguir instrucciones complejas. En la parte de programación, Muse Wonder y Wonder Full pueden desarrollar desde aplicaciones pequeñas hasta proyectos complejos . La IA es capaz de llevar un seguimiento de requisitos, modificaciones de código, pruebas y revisiones continuas sin perder el hilo, ya que fueron entrenados con tareas largas y variadas. Muse Wonder maneja mejor tareas nuevas o aquellas que no estuvieron presentes durante el entrenamiento, algo que sería indispensable en el terreno de los agentes. Muse Wonder Full supera a Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra y Gemini 4 Argon en el Índice de Inteligencia de Artificial Analysis, aunque todavía queda por detrás de Claude Opus 5.5. Esto representa un salto brutal si consideramos que hace un año los modelos de Meta no podían competir con Anthropic, OpenAI y las empresas chinas. Este avance también implica que la empresa ahora tiene que cuidar que las cosas no se salgan de control y sus agentes terminen afectando a terceros, como lo que ocurrió hace unos meses con Hugging Face . Sobre esta línea, Meta afirma que entrenó a Muse Wonder para no compartir información privada sin permiso , rechazar peticiones dañinas y resistir instrucciones manipuladoras. Los nuevos modelos tienen protección reforzada frente a abusos relacionados con ciberseguridad y salvaguardas en ámbitos químicos, biológicos, radiológicos y nucleares. Muse Wonder estará disponible a partir de hoy a través de la API de Meta y de Muse Code, mientras que Muse Wonder Full solo se ofrecerá a los suscriptores de Muse Code. La tecnológica confirmó que sus nuevos modelos llegarán pronto a la app de Muse, aunque tendrán prioridad aquellos que paguen una membresía.

sources.name: Xataka
sources.title: Meta presenta Muse Wonder y Muse Wonder Full, sus modelos de IA más punteros para ponerse en la frontera de la tecnología
sources.text: Meta ha lanzado este lunes Muse Wonder y Muse Wonder Full, los primeros modelos de sus “Superintelligence Labs” que, según la compañía , se colocan a la vanguardia junto con los mejores modelos de OpenAI y Anthropic. Llegan en un momento en que Meta intenta demostrar que toda la oleada de despidos y la profunda reestructuración de su división de IA, puesta en marcha el año pasado, está dando sus frutos. Muy atrás. Meta se quedó atrás en la carrera de la IA después del fiasco de Llama 4 el año pasado. Desde entonces, sus rivales han avanzado con sistemas mucho más capaces. Mark Zuckerberg respondió creando Meta Superintelligence Labs y contratando a Alexandr Wang , el exdirector ejecutivo de Scale AI, y uno de los nombres propios más destacados de la IA, para liderarlo. Muse Wonder es la primera prueba real de si esa apuesta ha funcionado. De momento, si hablamos en términos económicos, los inversores han reaccionado positivamente. Y es que según Bloomberg , las acciones de Meta subieron hasta un 4,7 % tras la noticia. Qué hay de nuevo. Hay dos modelos . Muse Wonder será pronto el cerebro de Muse, la app de agentes de IA personales de Meta, para los suscriptores de los niveles mensuales de 20 y 100 dólares. Por otro lado está Muse Wonder Full, que se trata de la versión más potente y estará limitada a los suscriptores de Muse Code, la herramienta de programación de IA de Meta. De momento ésta no se ofrecerá a través de la API. Wonder en sí llegará a los desarrolladores a través de la API de modelos de Meta, con un precio de 4 dólares por millón de tokens de entrada y 20 dólares por millón de tokens de salida, lo que según TechCrunch lo sitúa aproximadamente al nivel de GPT-6 Sol o Claude Opus 5.5 . Las cifras. A falta de poner a prueba el modelo en profundidad, Meta afirma que la versión más grande del modelo supera a Claude Fable 5.1 de Anthropic y se sitúa justo por debajo de Claude Opus 5.5 en el Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , uno de los rankings de referencia para valorar modelos de IA. La compañía también afirma que supera al GPT-6 Astra de OpenAI y a ambos modelos de Anthropic en algunas pruebas especializadas, incluyendo trabajo con documentos legales y desarrollo de software. De momento, todas estas cifras proceden de las propias pruebas de Meta, así que debemos esperar a las pruebas independientes para hacernos una idea realmente de la potencia de estos nuevos modelos. La propuesta. Wang declaraba a Bloomberg que el resto de la industria se ha "centrado realmente en los agentes de programación", mientras que Meta quiere hacer que el caso de uso del agente personal "destaque de verdad". Y para ello hacen referencia a dos técnicas: Active Memory y Active Focus. Según cuenta la compañía, mientras que la primera mencionada permite al modelo retener lo que le importa a un usuario durante "días, semanas, meses", para que la gente no tenga que repetirse, la segunda está diseñada para mantener al modelo enfocado en un objetivo establecido durante tareas largas y complejas, evitando errores acumulativos que puedan encarecer la factura cuando se trabaja con agentes. ¿Y qué pasa con la seguridad? El lanzamiento se produce en medio de una preocupación generalizada por los agentes de IA descontrolados, un tema del que llevamos meses viendo ejemplos poco alentadores . Meta afirma que ha entrenado a Muse Wonder para rechazar solicitudes peligrosas, como ayuda con armas biológicas o nucleares, un “mal uso cibernético” y otros asuntos, y ha publicado un marco para escalar las capacidades “de manera responsable”. Sin embargo, cabe señalar que Meta no ha dicho si los agentes que se ejecutan en el modelo se comportaron de forma errática en las pruebas, ni cómo abordaron este riesgo específicamente. La compañía tampoco ha revelado cómo se construyeron o entrenaron los modelos, más allá de afirmar, que el entrenamiento tuvo lugar en su centro de datos Prometheus en Ohio. Qué sigue. Wang declaraba a Bloomberg que su equipo ya está trabajando en "modelos más grandes y a mayor escala" mientras desarrolla versiones más baratas y especializadas de Wonder que podrían dar servicio a miles de millones de usuarios. Meta también ha afirmado que planea lanzar modelos más grandes de pesos abiertos, según comparten desde Wired, tras el pequeño Muse Glimmer .
